items.title: A missing context field never satisfies a constraint
items.body:
**Key: false: a missing context value never matches, even through not_in or inversion.**

The constraint code reads the field from the context and then, before looking at the operator, runs `if (!scalar(rawValue)) return false;`. A missing `plan` is `undefined`, which is not a scalar, so the constraint is false whatever the operator is. The comment states the rule: missing or invalid data must not turn a flag on through negation. The solutions chapter explains the danger: without that line, every context with no `plan` would pass `not_in [free]` and reach the rollout.

Why the others are wrong:
- *true, because absent is not 'free'*: that is the logic the guard exists to block.
- *error / 500*: the function returns `false`; it does not throw.
- *true only with inversion*: the guard runs before inversion is applied, so inversion cannot flip it.

excerpts.quote: const rawValue = ownValue(context, field); // Missing or invalid data must not become an enabled result through negation. if (!scalar(rawValue)) return false;
Rewrite it with `not_in [free]` and remove line 56, and every context *without* a `plan` field would pass the constraint and go on to the rollout check.

items.title: One revision number, If-Match, and a careful file commit
items.body:
Two editors can open the same flag. The app protects against one silently overwriting the other with **optimistic concurrency**: the whole workspace has one counter, `meta.version`, raised once per accepted change. Every admin write must send `If-Match` with the version the editor loaded. If the version on disk is different, the write is refused with 409 and the editor must reload.

Saving is also careful. `#commit` in `storage.js` writes the new JSON to a temporary file, flushes it to disk (`fsync`), then renames it over the real file. Renaming a file is atomic: other readers see either the old file or the new one, never half of each. A lock file (the "writer lease") stops two writers from committing at once.

While reading `mutate` and `#commit`, note two things: what is compared besides the version number, and at which exact line the new state becomes visible to readers.

excerpts.quote: | workspace revision | One counter for the whole workspace, raised once per accepted mutation.
| atomic replacement | Write a temporary file, then rename it over the real one.
this.io.writeFileSync(handle, bytes); this.io.fsyncSync(handle); this.io.closeSync(handle); handle = undefined; this.io.renameSync(temporary, this.dataFilePath);

items.title: Validating before authorizing leaks stored data
items.body:
**Key: a 422 describing the stored strategy is sent before the 403; authorize first, then validate.**

In `updateStrategy`, line 1158 validates the merged `{ ...strategy, ...input }` (which includes the *stored* strategy) before line 1160 checks project write access. A non-member with a bad body therefore gets a 422 whose message depends on the stored record, for example "only gradual rollout accepts parameters", which tells an outsider what kind of strategy it is. The fix in exercise 7 moves the validation below `requireProjectWrite`. The 404 for a missing id still comes first, which is accepted because ids are 12 random hex characters.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The full JSON is echoed*: the leak is in the message, not an echoed body.
- *Nothing leaks*: the write check is on line 1160, after validation.
- *The member list leaks in the 403*: the 403 message is the fixed "Project write access denied".

excerpts.quote: validateStrategySettings({ ...strategy, ...input }); const flag = getFlag(state, strategy.flagId); requireProjectWrite(state, actor, flag.projectId);
The 422 message was derived from the *stored* record ("only gradual rollout accepts parameters" tells an outsider that the strategy is not a gradual rollout).

items.title: The digest catches a hand edit that kept the version
items.body:
**Key: the digest comparison, so the next mutation gets 409.**

The commit condition has two halves: the version must match, *and* (when a digest is known) the SHA-256 digest of the file must match the one the server last accepted. A hand edit with an unchanged `meta.version` passes the first half but changes the file's bytes, so the digest differs and the next mutation is refused with 409. Without the digest, the server would write its stale draft over the hand edit and nobody would notice. `test/storage.test.js:124` covers this case.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing catches it*: the digest half does.
- *The version comparison*: the editor did not change the version, so that half still matches.
- *The writer lease*: a text editor does not create the lease file; the lease only coordinates writers inside the app.

excerpts.quote: (expectedDigest !== null && current.digest !== expectedDigest)
The digest half of the condition (`storage.js:294`) catches an edit made *without* bumping the version, such as someone hand-editing `data/state.json` in an editor.

items.title: A revoked token fails on the very next call
items.body:
**Key: 401: the wrapper re-reads the token on every call and requires it unrevoked.**

Every service method is wrapped. On each call the wrapper looks in the *current* state for a token with the same id and hash and `revokedAt === null`. After revocation `revokedAt` is set, so no token matches and `assert(token, 401, "Invalid token")` fails. The old `actor` object in the client's hands does not matter, because the server never trusts it on its own.

Why the others are wrong:
- *200, authenticated at session start*: the wrapper does not reuse earlier results.
- *200 until the cached actor expires*: there is no actor cache; the lookup happens on every call.
- *403, read access kept*: the token lookup fails before any scope or permission check, and that failure is a 401.

excerpts.quote: item.id === actor?.token?.id && item.hash === actor?.token?.hash && item.revokedAt === null, ); assert(token, 401, "Invalid token");
If a token is revoked between two requests, the next call fails with 401 even though the caller still holds an `actor` object from earlier.

items.title: Start here: a feature-flag admin app stored in one JSON file
items.body:
This pack uses a feature-flag platform. A feature flag is a named on/off decision (for example "is the checkout redesign enabled?"). Admins edit flags, rules and tokens; client apps send a user context and get a decision back. The whole workspace is one JSON file, so there is no database to learn first.

Suggested reading order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md`: the glossary table. Each term (workspace revision, If-Match, conflict, scope, membership, snapshot, bucketing) points to the exact lines that implement it.
2. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: follow one flag from the form to the saved file.
3. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: the core of this pack. Read every section; most quizzes come from it.
4. `astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`: how to reproduce stale edits, uncertain creations and stuck leases.
5. `astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md`, then `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` only after you tried the exercises.

Open each cited line in `src/` as you go; the guides' line numbers were checked against this version.

excerpts.quote: A feature flag is a named decision, such as whether a checkout redesign is enabled. Administrators create its configuration; applications submit a user context and receive a decision.
Complete [the practice assignments](05-PRACTICE.md) before reading [solutions and review](06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md).

readMore.why: The glossary: every key term with the file and lines that implement it.
The map of the app, including the table of deletion rules.

items.title: Variant weights: a rule about the set, with mixed status codes
items.body:
**Key: each 60 is valid alone; only the sum breaks the rule, and it answers 422 in the contract but 400 or 409 in the service.**

A single-field check looks at one value: is 60 an integer in range? Yes. The rule "weights add up to 100" is about the whole set of sibling variants, so it needs a check that sums them, like the `reduce` in `contracts.js`. The guide points out that this rule lives in two places with different answers: the contract rejects a bad sum with 422, while the service's `assertVariantWeights` answers 400 for a bad sum and 409 for a duplicate name. The review (R3) recommends 422 for all of them.

Why the others are wrong:
- *60 is out of range*: 60 is a valid weight on its own.
- *Only checked in the browser*: both the contract and the service check the sum.
- *Normalized at evaluation time*: no code rescales weights; a bad set is refused.

excerpts.quote: result.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.weight, 0) !== 100 ) reject(field, "variant weights must sum to 100");
An integer weight of 60 is valid on its own. Two sibling weights of 60 break the rule that variants sum to 100, and no single-field check can see that.

readMore.why: Exercise 4 notes: why mixed 422/400/409 answers stop a client from telling a conflict from a bad request.

items.title: Why check-then-act is safe here: frozen snapshot plus 409
items.body:
**Key: checks use the request's frozen snapshot, and the commit is refused (409) if version or digest changed.**

"Check-then-act" is risky when the data can change between the check and the write. Here the service's checks run against the snapshot the request started with. Then `mutate`, holding the lease, re-reads the file and compares its version and digest with what the request expected. Revision 9 is on disk but the request expected 8, so it throws 409 "State changed; reload and review before saving". So a check never approves a write on data that has changed since.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The lease blocks reads while a form is open*: the lease is held only for the moment of commit and never blocks readers.
- *Not safe, silent overwrite*: the version comparison stops exactly that.
- *Checks re-run after the write and revert*: nothing is written when the comparison fails, so there is nothing to revert.

excerpts.quote: current.state.meta.version !== expectedVersion || (expectedDigest !== null && current.digest !== expectedDigest) ) { this.#accept(current); throw storageError( 409, "State changed; reload and review before saving",
The checks never run against data that changed after they passed.

items.title: Why a 304 keyed on the snapshot ETag would be a bug
items.body:
**Key: the ETag names the configuration, not the caller; one snapshot gives different users different answers.**

A 304 Not Modified tells the client "reuse the answer you already have". The snapshot cache key is project, environment, version and digest. None of these says who asked. In the guide's example, one snapshot (one ETag) gives four different results for four contexts: user d on pro is in the 25% rollout, user a on pro is outside it, a free user fails the segment, and a context with no userId cannot be bucketed. A 304 would hand user A the decision cached for user D.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Decisions are identical for all users*: the table shows they are not.
- *The cache evicts quickly*: eviction is not the problem; the key itself is too coarse.
- *ETags change on every request*: the ETag changes only when the configuration changes, which is exactly why it cannot describe a user.

excerpts.quote: const key = JSON.stringify([ projectId, environmentId, state.meta.version, digest, ]);
One ETag maps to four different answers. A 304 response keyed on the ETag would therefore give user A user D's decision.

readMore.why: Section 4 walks through fixing this context-cache defect.

items.title: Publish in memory only after the file is safely replaced
items.body:
**Key: otherwise readers could see a change that a later disk failure rolled back.**

`#commit` does the disk work first: write the temp file, `fsync`, close, `renameSync` over the real file. Only then does it call `#accept`, which makes the new state the one readers get. If it published first and the write or rename then failed, readers would already have seen (and maybe acted on) a change that was never saved. The guide's heading says it in four words: durability and visibility are separate events.

Why the others are wrong:
- *renameSync is asynchronous*: it is the synchronous version (the `Sync` suffix); ordering is a choice, not a wait.
- *renameSync deletes the lease file*: it renames the temp file onto the data file; the lease is handled by `#withLease`.
- *The cache is cleared during the write*: nothing clears it; the order exists to keep memory from running ahead of disk.

excerpts.quote: this.io.renameSync(temporary, this.dataFilePath); created = false; // Publish only after successful replacement, using the exact JSON representation. return this.#accept({
If memory were published first, readers could see a change that a disk failure later rolled back.

items.title: Why the variant hash uses a different input
items.body:
**Key: so variant choice is independent of rollout position.**

Rollout bucketing hashes `"GROUP:USER" (group id, colon, user id)`. Users who get in at a 25% rollout are the ones with low buckets. If variant choice reused that same hash, being in the rollout would push users towards whichever variant covers the low numbers. Hashing a different string, `"variant:FLAGKEY:USER"`, gives an unrelated number, so being inside the rollout does not bias the variant. Both hashes are deterministic, so the same user always gets the same result and nothing needs storing.

Why the others are wrong:
- *MD5 versus SHA-256*: both go through `bucketValue`, which uses SHA-256 via `stableHash`.
- *Changes every request*: the input has no time or randomness, so it is stable.
- *Stored per user*: the guide says "nothing is stored"; the hash is recomputed.

excerpts.quote: const bucket = bucketValue( `variant:${flagKey}:${stickinessValue}`, totalWeight, );
Being inside the rollout therefore does not bias which variant you get.
return crypto.createHash("sha256").update(String(value)).digest("hex");

items.title: Who are you, what kind of action, and where
items.body:
The concepts guide splits access control into three separate questions. Keep them apart in your head:

- **Authentication**: which stored token (and user) does this request belong to? The server hashes the bearer string and looks for a matching token that has not been revoked.
- **Scope**: what *kind* of operation may this token do? The scopes are `read`, `write`, `admin` and `evaluate`.
- **Project membership**: *where* may this user act? This is a separate table of which users belong to which projects, with a role in each.

A useful exercise before the quizzes: for one write call, find each of the three checks in `src/server/services.js` (`getActorFromToken`, `requireScope`, `canWriteProject`) and note which status code each one produces when it fails. Then ask what happens when only one of the three is satisfied.

excerpts.quote: A token **scope** limits the *kind* of operation. **Project membership** decides *where* the user may perform it.
| scope | What a token is allowed to do: `read`, `write`, `admin` or `evaluate`. |

readMore.why: The full section, with the requireProjectWrite code and the roles that bypass membership.

items.title: Buckets run 1..100 so 0% and 100% mean what they say
items.body:
**Key: so rollout 0 enables nobody and rollout 100 everybody.**

`bucketValue` returns `(numeric % range) + 1`, so every user lands in 1..100. A rollout matches when `bucket <= rollout`. At rollout 0, no bucket is <= 0, so nobody is in. At rollout 100, every bucket is <= 100, so everybody is in. If the range were 0..99, bucket 0 would pass `<=` at rollout 0, and a "0%" rollout would still enable about one user in a hundred.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Bucket 100 reserved for testers*: no code treats bucket 100 specially.
- *Avoids the modulo*: the code does use `% range`; the `+ 1` only shifts the result.
- *A missing userId gets bucket 0*: a missing stickiness field is refused before bucketing ("Missing stickiness field").

excerpts.quote: const numeric = Number.parseInt(digest.slice(0, 12), 16); return (numeric % range) + 1;
With `matched: bucket <= rollout`, rollout 0 then enables nobody and rollout 100 enables everybody. With a 0..99 range, `<=` would let bucket 0 through at rollout 0.

items.title: PATCH with an empty description clears it and leaves stale alone
items.body:
**Key: description '' and stale still true.**

`updateFlag` applies `description` when `input.description !== undefined`. An empty string is defined, so the description becomes `''`. `stale` is only touched when `input.stale !== undefined`; the PATCH does not mention `stale`, so it stays `true`. This is the point of the section: leaving a field out, sending `false`, and sending `""` are three different instructions.

Why the others are wrong:
- *stale reset to false*: omitted fields are never filled with defaults.
- *422 for an empty description*: the contract refuses an empty *name*, not an empty description.
- *Old text kept*: that would happen with a truthiness test (`if (input.description)`), which is used for `name` and `type` but not for `description`.

excerpts.quote: if (input.description !== undefined) target.description = input.description; if (input.type) target.type = input.type; if (input.stale !== undefined) target.stale = Boolean(input.stale);
A PATCH `{description: ""}` intentionally clears the description and leaves `stale` alone.

items.title: A write token is not enough without project membership
items.body:
**Key: 403: the write scope is not enough without a membership row for that project.**

`requireProjectWrite` runs three checks in order: the token has `write` scope (it does), the project exists (it does, so no 404), and `canWriteProject`. That last check returns true at once only for an `instance_admin`. Everyone else needs a member role *and* a `projectMembers` row with that role for this exact project. This user's row is for Checkout, not the other project, so the check fails with 403 "Project write access denied".

Why the others are wrong:
- *200*: scope says what kind of action; membership says where, and both are required.
- *401*: the token is valid and unrevoked; 401 is for authentication failures.
- *404*: the project exists; the 404 in this function is only for a missing project.

excerpts.quote: requireScope(actor, "write"); assert(getProject(state, projectId), 404, "Project not found"); assert( canWriteProject(state, actor, projectId), 403, "Project write access denied", );
const membership = getProjectMembership(state, actor.user.id, projectId);
